title: The Race to Prove the Invisible Hand
subtitle: McKenzie, Arrow and Debreu

sections.title: A price for every market
sections.text:
Welcome to ECON 803. This episode accompanies the General Equilibrium chapter of Victor Aguiar's notes. It uses synthetic narration.

Imagine an economy waking up tomorrow morning. Every household has a plan. Every firm has a plan. Each plan looks sensible at the prices people expect to face. But will those plans fit together? The bread people want to buy must be available. The labour firms want to hire must be supplied. Income comes from selling resources and receiving profits, so purchasing power itself depends on prices.

That is the problem of general equilibrium. Finding the best bundle at given prices is only the beginning. We now ask whether there are prices at which all those individually optimal choices are jointly feasible.

Our title is The Race to Prove the Invisible Hand. Treat that phrase as a question. Exactly what would it mean to prove it? That some compatible prices exist? That their allocation is efficient? That the outcome is fair? That prices will actually move toward it? Each question needs its own argument.

There is also a question about economics as a profession. When several researchers solve closely related problems, whose name becomes attached to the achievement? Today we meet Lionel McKenzie, Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu. Then we return to the mathematics you should be able to explain yourself.

sections.title: Before the finish line
sections.text:
The original Arrow and Debreu article starts from Walras's system of interconnected markets and acknowledges earlier existence results by Abraham Wald. Their project combined production, exchange and consumption in one model. This was a continuing mathematical programme, with important predecessors.

Writing one equation per market is insufficient. Consider two equations in two unknowns: the first says that x squared equals negative one, and the second says that y equals zero. Over the real numbers there is no solution. Counting equations tells us little about existence, and even less about positive prices or feasible consumption. Economics needs assumptions that do real mathematical work.

Till Düppe's study of the correspondence traces Arrow and Debreu's collaboration from February 1952 through preparation of their joint manuscript in 1953. His account also emphasizes their different intellectual interests. It is easy for a familiar pair of names to conceal a collaboration between distinct researchers.

Keep three dates separate whenever you hear a discovery story: when an idea was developed, when it was publicly presented, and when it appeared in print. They can produce different rankings. A fourth distinction matters too: two theorems may solve a common problem while having different assumptions and different proofs.

sections.title: McKenzie and the problem of credit
sections.text:
McKenzie's article appeared in the April 1954 issue of Econometrica. Its title was On Equilibrium in Graham's Model of World Trade and Other Competitive Systems. Arrow and Debreu's article appeared in July of the same year.

Roy Weintraub's archival reconstruction establishes several important distinctions. Debreu presented the joint work in Chicago on December twenty seventh, 1952; McKenzie presented at the same meeting on December twenty ninth. McKenzie submitted his manuscript earlier and published first. Both contributions received contemporary recognition, while McKenzie's later visibility diminished.

There is an uncomfortable editorial detail. Debreu was asked to referee McKenzie's manuscript after submitting the joint paper. In a later letter he acknowledged the awkward position and described trying to assess it fairly. Those records support questions about conflicts of interest and scientific credit. They do not establish plagiarism or intentional suppression.

The methods also differed. McKenzie used demand and Kakutani's theorem. Arrow and Debreu worked through an abstract economy and Debreu's social equilibrium result. A shared research question does not make the arguments identical.

Historical interpretation remains contested. M. Ali Khan's later review challenges important aspects of Düppe and Weintraub's account and draws attention to other contributors, including Gale, Nikaido and Uzawa. The profession's familiar labels are a useful starting point for inquiry, but a poor stopping point.

Ask yourself what credit should recognize: public priority, mathematical generality, a reusable method, independent discovery, or influence on later work. Those criteria can point in different directions.

sections.title: The economic loop
sections.text:
Now return to the economy in the notes. A pure exchange economy begins with consumers, preferences and endowments. An endowment is a bundle of goods a consumer initially owns. At given prices, its market value determines that consumer's income.

For each price vector, solve every consumer's utility maximization problem. Add their chosen bundles, then subtract the total endowment. The result is aggregate excess demand. Positive excess demand for a good means desired purchases exceed the available quantity. Negative excess demand means some supply remains.

Prices enter twice. They determine what goods cost, and they determine the value of what households own. That income channel is why we cannot simply take a downward sloping demand curve from partial equilibrium and declare the whole system solved.

Only relative prices matter in this exchange model. With two goods we can choose prices that sum to one. Write the first price as s and the second as one minus s. We have reduced the price problem to a line.

Walras's law gives a second useful restriction: the value of aggregate excess demand is zero when everyone exhausts the budget. At strictly positive prices, if the first market clears in a two good economy, that identity forces the second market to clear as well. It is an accounting relation that helps us read equilibrium, rather than a reason every price must already be an equilibrium.

sections.title: A crossing you can calculate
sections.text:
Use exactly the worked economy from Chapter eleven. Consumer one owns one unit of good one and three units of good two. Consumer two owns three units of good one and one unit of good two. Each consumer's utility is the square root of the product of the two quantities consumed.

This utility gives equal expenditure shares. Each person spends half of income on each good. With normalized prices s and one minus s, total wealth is four. Aggregate demand for good one is therefore two divided by s. Since four units are available, excess demand for good one is two divided by s, minus four.

At s equal to one half, this excess demand is zero. The second market clears too. Both consumers choose two units of each good. We have solved the economy directly.

Now translate that calculation into fixed point language. The notes define an updated first price by adding one thirty second of excess demand to the current first price. Call this map T. A fixed point is a price at which the update changes nothing. Since the step size is positive, that happens exactly when excess demand for good one is zero.

On the closed interval from one tenth to nine tenths, this particular map is continuous and stays inside the same interval. A continuous function from a closed interval into itself must cross the forty five degree line. At that crossing, T of s equals s. The mathematical crossing therefore identifies a clearing price.

Pause here and draw the two curves yourself. The diagonal records unchanged prices. The other curve records the constructed update. Explain aloud why their intersection has economic meaning. You have already found the intersection algebraically; the existence argument explains why a crossing has to occur under the stated conditions.

sections.title: What the theorem needs
sections.text:
In many dimensions the geometry becomes harder to draw, but the strategy remains: construct an appropriate map, prove that it satisfies a fixed point theorem, then show that its fixed points solve the economic problem. Each of those steps carries an obligation.

Brouwer's theorem applies to a continuous function from a nonempty compact convex subset of finite dimensional Euclidean space into itself. Compactness controls escape. Convexity makes straight line combinations stay in the domain. Continuity prevents jumps. These are properties to verify for the actual construction.

The main theorem in the notes is a sufficient result for a finite pure exchange economy. Its assumptions include strictly positive individual endowments and continuous, strictly convex, strongly monotone preferences. Strict convexity gives unique demand when the problem has a solution. Existence and continuity of that demand still require attention to the feasible sets.

Zero prices are particularly delicate. A free desirable good can make the ordinary budget set unbounded. The proof uses artificially capped consumption sets to obtain a well behaved auxiliary problem, then proves that the cap does not affect the equilibrium eventually obtained. Appendix B supplies those details. Simply calling the price simplex compact would leave a gap.

If optimal choices are not unique, demand is a correspondence: one price vector can have several optimal bundles. Kakutani provides a suitable fixed point framework under additional properties of that correspondence, including nonempty convex compact values and upper hemicontinuity. Appendix B gives this extension.

The short theorem in the chapter and its fuller appendix belong together. Start by understanding the economic claim. Then inspect where each hypothesis enters. The original 1954 arguments have their own constructions; the chapter's Brouwer route is a teaching route through the problem.

sections.title: What existence leaves open
sections.text:
The introduction to Arrow and Debreu's paper explicitly leaves uniqueness and stability outside its investigation. That boundary is a useful discipline for your own proofs.

Existence says that at least one configuration satisfies the model. Uniqueness asks whether there is only one. A stability claim requires an adjustment rule and an argument about its behaviour over time. A fixed point can exist even when repeated application of a particular update fails to reach it. A diagram showing a crossing cannot settle that dynamic question.

Efficiency is another question. A welfare theorem connects equilibrium to Pareto efficiency under its own assumptions. Pareto efficiency means that no feasible change can help someone without hurting someone else. An extremely unequal allocation can satisfy that criterion. Equity requires additional judgments and, often, different policy questions.

Existence also does not prove that the model describes a particular market accurately. Empirical relevance requires evidence about institutions, preferences, technologies and behaviour. Nor does our finite commodity argument automatically establish equilibrium when the commodity space becomes infinite dimensional. That extension requires its own analysis.

The achievement is substantial precisely because the claim is precise: under specified conditions, individually optimal plans can fit together at common prices. Once that consistency is established, we can investigate welfare, comparative statics, computation and institutions without assuming that the model's defining equations are impossible to satisfy.

sections.title: Your reading task
sections.text:
For the week of November ninth to thirteenth, begin with Section eleven point three, Existence through a continuous price map. Review the Edgeworth box and aggregate excess demand sections immediately before it as needed. Then read Appendix B to see how the proof handles boundary prices, the artificial cap and nonunique demand.

Use three passes. First, state the theorem in ordinary language. Second, draw the proof as a sequence of claims, with the assumptions written beside the steps they justify. Third, close the notes and reconstruct the two consumer example by hand.

For your own preparation, write a short answer to five questions. Why is counting equations insufficient? What makes the price map eligible for Brouwer? Why does its fixed point imply market clearing? What changes when demand is not unique? And which claim about the invisible hand would still need another theorem?

These are study prompts, with no additional submission required for this activity. The separate problem set on the firm and partial equilibrium remains due Friday, November thirteenth.

Finally, return to the historical question. How would you describe the contributions of McKenzie, Arrow and Debreu without collapsing them into a single name or turning the story into an unsupported accusation? Precision matters when we write a proof, and it matters when we assign credit. Bring that same care to your reading.
